newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Chinese wheat import quotas halted trade says.
newsitem.headline: Chinese wheat import quotas halted trade says.

text.p: China has stopped issuing quotas for wheat imports following a bumper grain harvest and may not reconsider wheat import quotas until April 1997, traders in Hong Kong, China and Singapore said on Thursday.

"Our understanding on the wheat is that all quota on the wheat has stopped, they won't reconsider any quota until April 1st, 1997 fiscal year and that will give them time to re-evaluate the local situation," a trader in Singapore said.
"Between now and then, imports will be zero," he added.
An official contacted at China's Ministry of Internal Trade said he had no information on the ban.
"The Chinese government issued the ban about a month ago and the markets have been very quiet," said a Hong Kong trader.
Traders said the curtailment of imports had been kept very quiet and that the Ministry of Internal Trade had not made any formal announcements.
"All orders for wheat just stopped around October," a grains trader at a Chinese state-run firm in Hong Kong said.
The ban was issued because China had a bumper wheat harvest this year of 110 million tonnes, one trader said.
China also has roughly two million tonnes in reserves left over from last year's wheat imports, meaning total supplies were plentiful, the trader said.
The Chinese government is currently holding year-end meetings evaluating wheat supply and demand in the country's provinces to formulate the import programme for 1997, grains sources said.
One source said China should have an import plan for next year by the end of December, but added that wheat imports also depended on the international market.
China's wheat purchases, from June this year, have totalled 2.4 million tonnes, the trader said.
"Between June 1996 and May 1997 it will be closer to four million tonnes," he said.
Some traders said the import ban is directed at U.S. wheat and has been linked to the unresolved TCK smut fungus issue.
China refuses to accept wheat from the Pacific northwest of the United States because the U.S. Department of Agriculture cannot guarantee that grain from that area is TCK-free.
Grain traders have cut their import estimates for China across the board for calendar year 1997 on the basis of reports of a spectacular grain harvest.
Traders expect international wheat prices, already under pressure from bumper harvests around the world, to feel a further downward tug if China's wheat ban persists.

China imported 6.85 million tonnes of wheat in the first ten months of 1996, down 17.1 percent from the same period last year, according to customs figures. China imported 510,000 tonnes of wheat in October alone, the figures showed.
